extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or graduate students studying mathematical logic (second-order logic, model theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes syntactic and semantic results about second-order logic, Skolemization, Herbrand expansions, many-sorted logic, and 'general structures' as presented in a mathematical logic textbook (theorems, examples, and proof sketches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of satisfaction to predicate and function variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Let V be the set of all variables (individual, predicate, or function). An assignment s maps each variable to a suitable object: s(v) ∈ universe, s(Xn) is an n-ary relation on |A|, s(Fn) is an n-ary operation. For a term t, s(t) is defined naturally; for predicate variable X, |=_A X t1 ... tn[s] iff s(t1),...,s(tn) ∈ s(X). Quantifiers over predicate and function variables are evaluated by ranging over all relations/functions on |A|: e.g., |=_A ∀Xn_i ϕ[s] iff for every n-ary relation R on |A| we have |=_A ϕ[s(Xn_i | R)].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the values of s on variables free in the formula matter. For sentences, truth in a structure is unambiguous. This extends the usual first-order satisfaction clauses to second-order variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation comprehension formulas (Example 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any formula ϕ in which the predicate variable Xn does not occur free, the formula ∃Xn ∀v1...∀vn [Xn v1...vn ↔ ϕ] is valid: it asserts there exists a relation consisting of exactly the n-tuples satisfying ϕ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous function comprehension formulas are valid: if ψ defines a unique vn+1 for each v1...vn (i.e., ∀v1...vn ∃!vn+1 ψ), then ∃Fn ∀v1...vn+1 (Fn v1...vn = vn+1 ↔ ψ) is valid. These show existence of relations/functions defined by formulas (no free occurrence of the relation/function variable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order sentence for well-ordering (Example 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-ordering can be expressed by the second-order sentence ∀X (∃y Xy → ∃y (Xy ∧ ∀z (Xz → y ≤ z))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that second-order logic can capture global combinatorial properties (here: 'every nonempty subset has a least element') that are not first-order expressible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peano induction as a second-order sentence (Example 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The induction postulate is expressed as ∀X (X0 ∧ ∀y (Xy → XSy) → ∀y Xy). Any model of S1, S2, and this second-order induction postulate is isomorphic to (N;0,S) (i.e., the axioms are categorical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts second-order induction (ranges over all subsets) with first-order axiom schema; second-order induction enforces categoricity of the natural numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order least-upper-bound characterization of the reals (Example 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The least-upper-bound property of the real ordered field can be translated into a second-order sentence (expressing that every bounded nonempty set has a least upper bound). Any ordered field satisfying this second-order sentence is isomorphic to the ordered field of real numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that completeness/LUB is second-order expressible and yields categorical characterization of the reals among ordered fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order sentences characterizing infiniteness (Example 5, λ_∞)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are second-order sentences expressing 'the domain is infinite', e.g., λ_∞ = ∃X [∀u∀v∀w (Xuv → Xvw → Xuw) ∧ ∀u ¬Xuu ∧ ∀u ∃v Xuv], or using a function variable: ∃F [∀x∀y (Fx = Fy → x = y) ∧ ∃z ∀x Fx ≠ z] (there is an injective non-surjective function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These give second-order characterizations of infiniteness and are used to show consequences such as failure of compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: THEOREM 41A: Failure of compactness in second-order logic
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an unsatisfiable set of second-order sentences every finite subset of which is satisfiable. Example: {¬λ_∞, λ2, λ3, ...} where λ_n say 'there are at least n elements' and λ_∞ says 'infinite'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This demonstrates that the compactness theorem for first-order logic does not extend to full second-order logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: THEOREM 41B: Löwenheim–Skolem fails for second-order logic
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a second-order sentence in the language of equality that is true in a set iff its cardinality is 2^{ℵ0}. By encoding the real-ordered-field characterization and existentially quantifying its parameters, one obtains a sentence characterizing continuum cardinality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike first-order logic, second-order logic can pin down specific infinite cardinalities; hence Löwenheim–Skolem (downward/ upward) fails for full second-order semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: THEOREM 41C: Nondefinability and non-enumerability of valid second-order sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of Gödel numbers of valid second-order sentences is not definable in N by any second-order formula. Consequently, the set of Gödel numbers of second-order validities is not arithmetical and not recursively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the second-order theory T^2 of N and a reduction via the second-order Peano conjunction α: σ ∈ T^2 iff (α → σ) is valid. So enumerability and definability results for first-order do not extend to second-order validities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison: second-order universal sentence vs first-order axiom schema (induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A second-order universal sentence (like the induction postulate) quantifies over all subsets, so if a structure A satisfies it, every subset containing 0 and closed under successor is all of |A|. In contrast, the corresponding first-order schema only guarantees this for definable subsets (there may be undefinable subsets violating induction). Example: models with Z-chains satisfy the first-order schema but not second-order induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights semantic strength of second-order universal sentences compared to merely having all first-order instances (axiom schema).

rubrics_metrics.name: SKOLEM NORMAL FORM THEOREM
rubrics_metrics.description: For any first-order formula, one can find a logically equivalent prenex second-order formula of the special form: (a) a (possibly empty) string of existential individual and function quantifiers, followed by (b) a (possibly empty) string of universal individual quantifiers, followed by (c) a quantifier-free formula. Example: ∀x∃y ϕ(x,y) is equivalent to ∃F ∀x ϕ(x, F x) (use of Skolem functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction uses choice to pick Skolem functions in a model; the theorem provides a systematic Skolemization method used in satisfiability/validity reductions and in later corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: COROLLARY 42A: Reduction of satisfiability to universal formulas with function symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: For any first-order ϕ, one can find a universal formula θ in an expanded language containing function symbols such that ϕ is satisfiable iff θ is satisfiable. The method: convert ϕ to Skolem form ∃y1 ∃F2 ... ∀x1... ψ and replace existential parameters by new function symbols/constants to form θ (a universal sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduction lets one focus satisfiability decision problems on universal sentences (with function symbols). Applying to ¬ϕ yields an existential (with function symbols) formula equivalent for validity testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: COROLLARY 42B: Undecidability consequences from Skolemization
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) The set of Gödel numbers of satisfiable universal (first-order) sentences is not recursive. (b) The set of Gödel numbers of valid existential (first-order) sentences is not recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: using Corollary 42A, deciding satisfiability/validity in these restricted forms would decide arbitrary validities (contradicting Church's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicate-variable Skolemization variant (∀2/∃2 reductions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using predicate variables instead of function variables, any first-order formula is logically equivalent to a second-order formula consisting of (a) existential predicate quantifiers, (b) universal individual quantifiers, (c) existential individual quantifiers, followed by (d) a quantifier-free formula. Corresponding corollaries reduce satisfiability to ∀2 formulas (with predicate symbols) and validity to ∃2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a cost in form complexity, but this yields alternative reductions and decidability/undecidability comparisons (see corollaries and exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: HERBRAND'S THEOREM and Herbrand expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a set Γ of first-order formulas (no equality for simplicity), replace each by an 'equally satisfiable' set Γ' of universal formulas in Skolemized language. Let H be the Herbrand universe (all ground terms). Let Inst(Γ') be the set of all ground instances obtained by substituting terms from H for universally quantified variables. Then either (I) Inst(Γ') is unsatisfiable in propositional logic and Γ |= ϕ; or (II) Inst(Γ') is satisfiable (truth assignment v) and one builds a Herbrand model H (with |H| = H and interpreting predicate atoms by v) witnessing Γ' satisfiable and giving a countermodel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure reduces first-order satisfiability to checking propositional satisfiability of finite ground instances (compactness ensures finite witness). The constructive case provides Herbrand models and underlies completeness and enumerable-theory proofs; exercises discuss equality and enumerability consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many-sorted logic: syntax and semantics (Section 4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a set I of sorts. For each sort i, variables v^i_n, quantifier ∀_i, predicate/function/constant symbols typed by tuples of sorts; terms of sort i built inductively. A many-sorted structure A assigns a nonempty universe |A|_i to each sort i and interprets symbols with the appropriate domain/codomain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalizes many-sorted languages used to model multiple domains (e.g., individuals vs relations). Nothing essentially new compared to one-sorted case, but notation and bookkeeping differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of many-sorted logic to one-sorted logic (Qi-relativization and axioms (cid:19))
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate each many-sorted formula ϕ to one-sorted ϕ* by relativizing quantifiers: ∀_i v φ becomes ∀v (Q_i v → φ*). Convert a many-sorted structure A to one-sorted A* with universe ⋃_i |A|_i and Qi interpreted as |A|_i. Include axioms (cid:19) in the one-sorted language: (1) ∃v Q_i v for each i, and (2) closure axioms ensuring function symbols send Q_i1×...×Q_in into Q_{in+1}. Lemmas 43A/43B show truth preservation; Theorem 43C: (Σ |= σ) in many-sorted iff ((Σ)* ∪ (cid:19) |= σ* ) in one-sorted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduction allows carrying over compactness, enumerability, Löwenheim–Skolem from the one-sorted case to many-sorted languages; (cid:19) axioms ensure converting back is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for many-sorted logic: Compactness, Enumerability, Löwenheim–Skolem
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the reduction to one-sorted, infer: (a) Compactness: if every finite subset of a set Σ of many-sorted sentences has a model, then Σ has a model. (b) Enumerability theorem: For a recursively numbered many-sorted language, the set of Gödel numbers of valid sentences is r.e. (via Cn((cid:19))). (c) Löwenheim–Skolem: any many-sorted structure (countable language) has an elementarily equivalent countable structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each follows by applying the corresponding one-sorted theorem to Σ* ∪ (cid:19) and translating models back to many-sorted structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: General structures: viewing second-order as many-sorted first-order (Section 4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the second-order language as a many-sorted first-order language with sorts: one individual sort, and for each n>0 an n-place predicate sort and an n-place function sort. Introduce membership predicates ε_n (taking an n-place predicate variable and n individual terms) and evaluation function symbols E_n (taking an n-place function variable and n individual terms), so that ε_n(X, t1,...,tn) corresponds to X t1...tn and E_n(F,t1,...,tn) corresponds to F t1...tn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recasting lets one interpret the universes for predicate/function variables rather than fixing them as 'all relations/functions', giving 'general structures' semantics. Translate between the two languages by adding/removing ε_n and E_n.

rubrics_metrics.name: THEOREM 44A: Homomorphism to structure with genuine membership and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a structure A for the many-sorted language with disjoint universes, there exists a homomorphism h of A onto a structure B such that (a) h is identity on the individual universe (so satisfaction of formulas is preserved via h◦s), (b) the n-place predicate universe of B consists of certain n-ary relations over the individual universe and (R,a1,...,an) ∈ ε^B_n iff (a1,...,an) ∈ R, and (c) the n-place function universe of B consists of certain n-place functions on the individual universe with E^B_n(f,a1,...,an) = f(a1,...,an).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: map each predicate-sort element Q to the relation { (a1,...,an) | (Q,a1,...,an) ∈ ε^A_n }, and map function-sort element g to the function a ↦ E^A_n(g,a1,...,an). This shows without loss of generality one may assume ε_n is genuine membership and E_n genuine evaluation.
